If you're a photography lover and you own an iPhone, you probably have some thoughts on the way the camera processes images. So does Rian Johnson , director of the Knives Out franchise and Star Wars: The Last Jedi . This inspired him to team up with cinematographer Steve Yedlin to build an app that captures RAW image data and bypasses Apple’s regular photo processing.
“So I recently badgered my cinematographer Steve Yedlin into making my ideal iPhone still camera app,” Johnson wrote on X (formerly Twitter). “It shoots RAW, bypasses the iPhone’s look processing, and instead uses the same image processing we use on our movies.”
Named Chromagraph Camera , the app has been commended for its many capabilities, making users feel like they have a film camera in their pocket. The viewfinder is only meant to help you frame the shot, instead of showing you exactly how it will look. You can see the result after the image has been processed in your gallery. Users can also adjust color, exposure, and grain later in non-destructive edits, as the app stores full-quality RAW files.
“I’ve messed with plenty of good 3rd party tools but this is an elegant one-stop-shop, it just takes beautiful shots with Steve’s special sauce processing,” Johnson gushes. “I honestly just asked Steve (and our genius color science coder friend Eric Cameron) to make it because I take a ton of pics with my phone and wanted to have it for myself, and they figured hey, let’s put it out there. Hope you enjoy!”
While the response has been overwhelmingly positive, with many showing their experiments with the Chromagraph Camera on social media, Johnson shared that the app has a few caveats. For starters, it’s stills-only, and it’s only available on iPhone. “Huge apologies to my Android friends,” the director says. “Hardware consistency across Apple devices is part of what allows us to do this with confidence. Android devices are much more varied, and there’s no way with our small team we could dial it in for every device.”

items.desc: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.
items.text:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually , external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.
"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.

items.title: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
items.desc: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
items.text:
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.
It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.
"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.
"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The spacecraft - just seen here - has taken selfies as it has closed in on Mercury
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018 , launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.
So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.
A close up view of the scarred surface of Mercury
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon

Yu Hong , “Night Walk,” 2023 . Acrylic on canvas. 3 parts, each: 300 x 250 cm ; 3 parts, each: 118 ⅛ x 98 ⅜ in ; Overall: 300 x 750 cm; Overall: 118 ⅛ x 295 ¼ in. (Photo: © Yu Hong, courtesy of Lisson)
Drawing on the visual language of classical religious art, Chinese artist Yu Hong constructs dramatic scenes that reflect the instability of contemporary life. In a new exhibition, titled Field of Asura , monumental compositions inspired by European altarpieces anchor the presentation, placing the human figure at the center of an imagined world.
In the titular work, a towering column of bodies swirls through a three-part composition. Some figures appear to be swallowed by the mass, while others float above it on clouds. The title refers to the Asura realm in Buddhist and Hindu mythology, an astral world marked by perpetual battles between demigods and deities. Yu Hong draws on this mythology to reflect the ongoing struggles that define modern society.
Yu Hong looks to centuries of religious painting for inspiration, adapting familiar compositions to address contemporary experiences. Her subjects are often people from her own life, including friends and family members. This personal dimension grounds the fantastical scenes in recognizable human experiences.
Across the exhibition, Yu Hong gives particular attention to the physical expression of her subjects. Bodies twist and stretch across the canvas, conveying emotion through posture rather than facial expression. Many figures turn away from the viewer, shifting attention toward their gestures and physical relationships.
The presentation also includes Night Walk (2023), the exhibition’s only previously completed work. Referencing Pieter Bruegel the Elder’s The Blind Leading the Blind (1568), it depicts a procession moving through a landscape of fire and darkness. The scene evokes a collective passage into uncertainty, extending the exhibition’s exploration of human vulnerability.
By bringing historical painting into the present, Yu Hong creates a visual language that feels both familiar and unsettling.
Field of Asura is now on view at Lisson Gallery in New York through January 9, 2027.

items.text:
The children of an elderly Chinese mother have touched the hearts of millions by painstakingly building a new staircase by hand up the side of a mountain to help her reach her home more easily.
Her youngest daughter said that she remembers her mother holding their hands down the old mountain path in her childhood, and that now it was “their turn” to hold hers.
Born and raised on the top of a mountain in eastern China’s Zhejiang Province, the children moved their mother into town after their father died decades ago, where she alternated stays between her eldest and second-eldest son homes.
She never took to urban life. She missed living on the mountain, and Chinese custom required she return at least once a year in April for the Qingming Festival, or Tomb Sweeping Day.
On this day, millions of Chinese return to clean away overgrowth, leaves, and dirt accumulated on the graves of their family and ancestors—a central expression of the virtue of filial piety expounded in China since ancient times.
Yet the old path down which she would take her children hand-in-hand was now overgrown and disused—the haunt of snakes—according to the story reported first by Chao News on the mainland and published later in English by the South China Morning Post.
58-year-old Huang Zhulian decided it was now her and her older siblings’ turn to demonstrate their filial piety, and began to build what Chinese social media has celebrated as a “filial piety sky ladder.”
As it was Huang’s idea, she undertook planning and purchasing of materials before assuming the role of the foreman as they aimed to rebuild an older path up another side of the mountain with less foliage. Learning what was being undertaken, their mother contributed 50,000 RMB, or $7,500, from her savings to assist in the project.
Two of her brothers and two cousins carried stones up the mountain to the build site and mixed the cement. Huang’s sister and brother-in-law prepared meals and looked after the construction tools. Her nephew and niece helped clear away rubble whenever they were free, while her own son assisted his uncles with the clever use of a heavy-lift drone to move stones.
They worked between August and October to finish the path before winter, and succeeded in creating a 430-step route, which included portions quite literally fastened to the side of a sheer cliff.
Huang told Chao News she lost over 6 pounds during the work, got a tan, and lost a lot of hair, but has no regrets.

She first spoke about the importance of toys for kids. Beyond making them happy, she stressed how they support brain development. She believes toys also boost children’s imagination and spark their creativity. That’s why she says it’s important to consider all these nuances when designing toys.

Our expert noted that designers also consider the emotional connection a child can have with a toy. We often see little ones cradling stuffed animals and taking them everywhere they go, and that in itself is a sign of a good toy. She believes that when kids form this connection, it can have a lasting impact, making playtime more meaningful and memorable.
Sharanya also explained that to understand better how a child’s mind works, designers sometimes work with child psychologists. This gives them perspective on how to make a toy more intuitive and inviting. After all, kids should not be frustrated while using it; rather, it should be a seamless experience that lets them enjoy it.

Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”

items.text:
For artist Sara Silks , the natural world has always sparked curiosity and inspiration. Growing up exploring the woods and waterways of the Ozarks in the Midwestern United States, she developed a deep connection to the landscape. Today, that familiarity informs her growing concern over the environmental changes taking place around her.
Her series Warming Effects explores these changes through layered photographic compositions that combine images of extreme weather with geometric shapes and intricate patterns. Photographs of ice, fire, storms, and other natural phenomena become the foundation for abstract arrangements that explore the tension between nature’s visual beauty and the uncertainty of a changing climate.
Silks approaches photography as an experimental process, drawing on her background in drawing and printmaking to move beyond traditional documentation. She prints her compositions on handmade Unryu washi paper and applies a labor-intensive cold wax finish, giving each work a distinctive tactile surface.
My Modern Met had the chance to speak with Silks about the inspiration behind Warming Effects , her intuitive approach to image-making, and how she uses photography to navigate her concerns about the environment. Read on for our exclusive interview with the artist.

I had the freedom to investigate whatever caught my attention. Those hours of discovery and quiet observation created a feeling of oneness with the landscape that has stayed with me throughout my life.
When I photograph it, those memories are present in what I notice and how I respond. Changes in a place so deeply familiar feel personal. My concern for the landscape grows out of that attachment and increasingly finds its way into the work.

41 years ago today, US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet Union leader Mikhail Gorbachev met for the first time. The Geneva Summit in Switzerland was the first step toward a thawing of Cold War tensions, as Reagan and Gorbachev talked about all topics and got to know each other’s positions. The new relationship led to the signing two years later of the INF Treaty to eliminate intermediate-range nuclear weapons. READ more about the fruits of the meeting… (1985)
The summit also concluded with the Northern Pacific Air Safety accord that aimed at preventing a repeat of the Soviet downing of Korean Airlines Flight 007 in September 1983. A signing ceremony followed, with an agreement on the opening of consulates in Kiev and New York being signed, as well as agreements to renew regular US‑Soviet dialogue on future summit meetings. 41 cultural exchange agreements were also signed, including the restart of exchanges of theatrical and artistic groups and major art exhibits.
Both Reagan and Gorbachev came away from Geneva feeling that they had “started something”, with Reagan saying that the meetings in Geneva “expressed the will and desire of both sides to find answers that would benefit not only all the people of the world, but also the yet unborn”. Gorbachev agreed.
This was the predecessor of the Reykjavik Summit, where the Soviet Leader pitched Reagan on the elimination of all nuclear weapons. Reagan actually agreed, but disagreement arose surrounding the Strategic Defense Initiative—monikered “Star Wars.” This government boondoggle was already funded by the billions, and its potential to weaponize outer space was extremely disturbing to the Soviets. Gorbachev called for its delay by 10 years in exchange for total nuclear disarmament, but Reagan understood the political consequences of going against the entrenched interests at stake in Star Wars’ fraudulent development.
Reykjavik was likely the closest the world has come to ridding itself of nuclear weapons, and Geneva was a huge stepping stone towards that missed opportunity.

items.text:
Experts call trial results of medication that slowed cognitive decline by almost a third ‘very promising’
A pill that mimics Viagra by relaxing blood vessels and increasing blood flow to the brain can slow cognitive decline in people with Alzheimer’s disease by almost a third, a global study suggests.
Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050. There is currently no cure.
In a stage three trial spanning 13 countries, including the UK, researchers found the tablet AR1001 slowed decline by 31% in patients with early Alzheimer’s disease not receiving any other treatment.
Experts not involved with the study urged caution but said the results were “exciting” and “very promising” and could signal the arrival of a “totally new treatment” for Alzheimer’s.
The findings were presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston.
AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor and from the same family of medicines as Viagra, which is used to treat erectile dysfunction.
The South Korean company AriBio, which makes AR1001, said the drug slowed decline in 604 people taking no other drugs for Alzheimer’s. In a wider group of patients taking other drugs, the tablet did not achieve statistically significant results.
Prof Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow at the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the results looked “very promising”.
“This drug acts through boosting blood flow and likely also directly stimulating pathways in brain cells that promote learning and memory,” she said.
Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said the findings were “very encouraging”, and marked “an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments”.
AR1001 was “especially interesting” because it was an oral drug that took a “different approach” to existing treatments, she said. “Rather than targeting amyloid, it acts on a specific enzyme and influences several other processes involved in brain function.
“The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group.

items.title: Wildlife conservation cash targets ex-colliery sites
items.desc: The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards at sites in Yorkshire.
items.text:
The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards
Ponds are to be restored and freshwater habitats created for amphibians and reptiles at two former colliery sites in South Yorkshire.
The Froglife charity has been awarded nearly £890,000 of Lottery cash to carry out the work in Rother Valley, as well as at sites in North and West Yorkshire.
Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands were originally regenerated through the National Coalfields Programme after the pits there closed in the 1990s.
Sheila Grundry, from Froglife, said staff were "delighted" to work in the area because "freshwater will make a lasting difference for frogs and other wildlife and it's a great way for local people to learn new skills".
The £889,761 investment in Froglife's Coalface to Wildspace project will also help local communities connect with nature, according to the charity.
Dinnington Woodland is one of the sites in Yorkshire which will be a focus of the project
The aim of the project across Yorkshire is to create 48 new ponds, improve 93 existing freshwater habitats and establish new "neighbourhood wildlife corridors" like small ponds and bug hotels.
These "corridors" will act as stepping stones for local wildlife from insects to birds, providing food, shelter and water to improve biodiversity across former industrial sites and help wildlife move between one habitat and another.
Conservationist Andy Goff, project manager in Yorkshire, said the transformation of the sites would be for everyone.
"We want people to engage with the nature that is on their doorstep and wildlife in general," he explained.
"I'm really excited about getting people involved from all over Yorkshire."
The Coalface to Wildspace project is funded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund for the next four years, with Froglife having already run similar projects in the Midlands and Scotland.
Rother Valley MP Jake Richards said the project was important for the area.
"These former industrial sites are an important part of our area's history," he said.
"This project will help transform them into thriving habitats while creating opportunities for local people to get involved."

101 years ago today, Robert F. Kennedy was born. The US Senator from New York became Attorney General during his brother John Kennedy’s years in the White House—and would eventually launch his own race for president after JFK’s assassination. READ more… (1925)
Many of the civil rights initiatives championed by the Kennedy Administration and its successor were spearheaded by RFK, who was also known as “Bobby” .
On the night that Martin Luther King Jr. was shot and killed, Robert F Kennedy delivered the news to the people of Indianapolis, Indiana. Local police warned him that a riot could break out there in the heart of an African-American ghetto. He wrote his notes on the ride over and started his speech without any drafts, delivering it on the back of a Flatbed truck. Although all major US cities experienced riots, Indianapolis remained calm, thanks to RFK’s speech.
63 days after that night, RFK was assassinated at age 42 while campaigning for the Presidency. Since his death in 1968, his wife Ethel raised their 11 children and never remarried. She oversaw the Robert F. Kennedy Center for Justice & Human Rights until her death last year.
75 years ago today, Snowdonia National Park was created by British Parliament as the third national park in the country after the Lake and the Peak districts. It protects a mountainous region in northern Wales of the same name of 827 square miles of myth-shrouded mountains and valleys. Much of the park is undeveloped, but there are also many agricultural activities that go on.
The English name for the area derives from Snowdon, which is the highest mountain in Wales at 3,560 feet (1,090 meters). In Welsh, the area is named Eryri. A commonly held belief is that the name is derived from eryr (“eagle”), and thus means “the abode/land of eagles.”

A one-time infusion of CRISPR gene editing therapy slashed dangerous cholesterol by 52%, with the patients still experiencing the benefit 12 months after initial treatment, and without side effects.
The Cleveland Clinic in Ohio reported that their Phase 1 human trial showed a one-time infusion of a gene-editing therapy using CRISPR-Cas9 was effective and safe in reducing “bad” LDL cholesterol and triglycerides by nearly half in patients throughout a one-year follow-up, after their disorder had previously been resistant to medication.
The trial, which included 15 patients, aimed to see if the reductions in LDL cholesterol and triglycerides previously reported after two months would persist for 12 months. After 12 months, patients who were treated with the highest dose saw a 52.5% lowering from baseline in LDL cholesterol, and a 47.8% reduction in triglycerides. There were no serious adverse events related to the therapy during the one-year follow-up.
The study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in August, was funded by CRISPR Therapeutics AG in Switzerland.
“The durability of the lipid-lowering effect was impressive,” said Cleveland Clinic cardiologist Dr. Luke Laffin, the first author of the study.
“It is encouraging that there were no serious safety events related to CTX310 in the trial and in the year following treatment. We look forward to continuing to investigate this therapy in a larger number of patients.”
CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing technology that can be used to modify or correct specific regions of a person’s DNA to treat serious diseases.
This trial tested CTX310, an experimental CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing treatment that is delivered as a one-time infusion. CTX310 carries the CRISPR editing mechanism into the liver, where it switches off a gene called ANGPTL3. Turning off this gene can lower LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which are both linked to heart disease.

A pub owner took advantage of the Christmas season, spending thousands on a festive light display to cheer up his town’s locals.
Christian Ogley says this year has been particularly tough for residents in the picturesque town of Knaresborough, England, as the cost of living soared.
“It has been a turbulent year for everyone in the area and across the UK to say the least, said the 34-year-old who owns Blind Jack’s pub in the historic North Yorkshire town set on cliffs above the River Nidd.
“I just wanted to do something nice to make people smile.”
So, in an attempt to spread some Christmas cheer, he’s spending around $6,000 on materials and electricity to erect the beautiful display on this two-story pub.
“So far it has seemed to have done that! We’ve had many compliments.”
With help from seven staff members and regulars, they spent the past week building and installing the design, which includes a 5-meter-tall tree as its (16-ft) centerpiece, surrounded by white lights imitating falling snow and huge red ribbons.
“To start it was just a bit of fun, but as I have been installing it so many people have been wanting to talk to me about it and have been posting it on social media.

Christian was inspired after visiting New York City and Ireland over the past two years and seeing the effort landlords put into their holiday displays.
He decided he would do the same at his watering hole—something which he says isn’t too common to see in the UK.
He started designing the mega Christmas project in January by sketching out initial ideas on the back of beer mats.
The dad-of-two who studied graphic design at university, even needed a cherry picker for the huge Christmas tree, made from wood and tarpaulin.
Altogether, it contains over 10,000 lights which he says costs him around £2.50 a day to run from 12 am to 12 pm.
“It is surprisingly cheaper than I thought to keep the lights on, which means I can keep them on for longer.
“The lights mean so much to me and the community, I’m trying to keep them glowing for as long as I can each day.”
Christian told SWNS news last week that he still isn’t finished yet, as he intends to install two seven-foot nutcrackers on the pavement.
He bought the pub in 2017 with his 33-year-old wife Alice Ogley, and last year it won an award for Best Beer Pub in the UK.
“Hopefully the display can become a bit of a tradition and something locals can look forward to every year.”

items.desc: The exhale from a whale’s blowhole has been captured by drones, and used to complete the genome sequencing of one of the ocean giants for the first time. items.text:
The exhale from a whale’s blowhole has been captured by drones, and used to complete the genome sequencing of one of the ocean giants for the first time.
Researchers from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland were part of an international team to sequence a whole genome using samples from whale breath collected by a small aerial drone.
It marks the first time sequencing has been completed without the use of physical interventions—commonly using darts and biopsies collected by boat, which disturbs the animals, or from stranded mammals or historical specimens.
In some places and for some species this isn’t possible.
Yet, genomic data is “critical” for conservation, enabling researchers to measure population health, genetic diversity and inbreeding, as well as to identify individuals for “mark-recapture” studies, determine sex, and estimate population size.
To overcome the collection challenge, the team attached sterile petri dishes to a small drone. ( See below… )
They flew it through the exhaled breaths of one humpback whale at a time, which typically has one to six breaths per surfacing.
They collected 58 blow samples from 26 individual humpback whales in the Kitimat Fjord System in northern British Columbia, Canada.
Around 84% of the DNA in the blow came from the whale itself.
Repeat samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across two years, gave matching genomes—with the most upwind whale in a group targeted, to avoid mixing DNA from different animals.
More than a third of samples required no boat at all—only flying the drone directly from land.
Before the new study, only one North Pacific humpback’s whole genome had ever been publicly available.
After collection, DNA was sequenced to produce low-coverage nuclear genomes—inherited from both parents—and high-coverage mitochondrial genomes, inherited just from the mother.
The research team also discovered genetic diversity estimated from blow was very similar to estimates from traditional biopsies—with this particular population showing no evidence of inbreeding beyond a shared ancestry or past population bottlenecks.

items.text:
Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing
A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.
In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.
Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally.
Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.
Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.
He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.
“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”

What's particularly fun about making things yourself is that you can play around with colors, materials, and designs until you get exactly what you want.

A 2025 Ipsos iSay survey of 1,000 US panel members found that 36% participated in arts and crafts, while 33% made their own home decorations. Instead of spending hours looking for something that matches your taste, sometimes it's easier (and more fun) to make it yourself.
Interestingly, getting crafty might also make us happier.
In 2024, researchers examined data from 7,182 adults in England. They found that people who engaged in arts and crafts reported greater happiness and life satisfaction. They were also more likely to feel that what they did in life was worthwhile. These associations remained even when researchers took age, employment, and financial circumstances into consideration.
Perhaps part of the appeal is having something tangible to show for our efforts.
Many of us spend eight hours a day working on a laptop. At the end of the day, switching off that screen and spending an hour knitting, painting, or working with clay can be a welcome change. items.title: Hormuz swim highlights environmental cost of war
items.desc: Ocean campaigner Lewis Pugh completes Hormuz challenge and warns of lasting environmental damage.
items.text:
Pugh said the Strait of Hormuz has an "extraordinary natural world" beneath the surface
A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the Strait of Hormuz to draw attention to what he says is the environmental cost of the conflict involving Iran.
Lewis Pugh, who is a UN Patron of the Oceans, swam about 15km (9.3 miles) through the strategic waterway, a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.
Pugh, 56, who was born in Plymouth, Devon said "war causes immense human suffering" but nature is "another casualty that receives far too little attention".
He is calling for an end to the fighting, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.
The Strait of Hormuz carries a significant share of global oil shipments from the Middle East
The swimmer is believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in March .
He swam from Musandam Island in the strait to the Cape of Hormuz, at the northern tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula.
According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, an oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 4km (2.5 miles) from where he was swimming on the first day.
On the second day, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from the burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier Tara Gas and later passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.
"My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers on board," Pugh said.
"The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences - not just for crew members, but also on the surrounding marine environment."
Pugh has completed long-distance swims in every ocean of the world
Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often receives less attention than the human cost.
"War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart, and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes," he said.
"But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped."
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.
Pugh said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

Antarctic blue whales have increased in number 1,000% since 1973 when the harpoons were finally hung up for good.
Growing from just 418 whales to 4,018, the superb recovery has averaged 4.5% per year.
Though the International Whaling Commission banned the killing of Antarctic blue whales in 1964, illegal whaling continued until 1973. These long-lived animals—the largest ever known to have existed—reproduce very slowly with just one calf every 3 years or so.
As impressive a comeback as the whales have made, counting 4,018 animals was also quite the impressive feat of data science.
Even though one can spot a blue whale with a satellite, the Southern Ocean population spends most of its time underwater.
Zoe Rand, a postdoctoral scholar in the University of Washington School of Marine and Environmental Affairs, lead a study that examined historical catch data, modern photo identification records, and decades of “line transect” surveys to estimate current population.
Line transect surveys from 1978 to 1984, 1985 to 1991, and 1991 to 2004 surveyed the entire Southern Ocean by sailing boats along straight lines and counting whales seen and the distances they remained from the boat.
These data sources not only indicated the number was growing, but that it has grown so substantially over time.

items.title: Oil firm fined for breaking environmental rules hundreds of times
items.desc: Ten charges involved oil, cyanide and other pollutants entering local waterways.
items.text:
Stanlow Oil Refinery, owned by Essar Energy, is the second largest refinery in Britain
One of the UK's largest oil refinery operators has been ordered to pay £873,473 after breaching environmental permit limits nearly 500 times over three years.
The Environment Agency (EA) said the Stanlow refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, exceeded wastewater discharge limits at least 489 times between 2018 and 2020. Essar Oil (UK) Limited pleaded guilty to 12 charges in March .
Essar Oil, which trades as EET Fuels, was fined £800,000 and ordered to pay £73,473 in costs at Warrington Magistrates' Court.
EET Fuels said it regretted the "historic incidents" and had invested more than £24m to improve environmental performance.
Ten charges related to wastewater discharges containing oil, suspended solids and chemicals, including cyanide, into Thornton Brook, the River Gowy and the Manchester Ship Canal.
Two other charges concerned incidents in 2019.
The Manchester Ship Canal runs for 36 miles from Eastham in Wirral to Salford
In February 2019, between 15 and 20 tonnes of a chemical leaked into the ship canal after a vent was left open and a written procedure was not followed.
A month later, a contractor's vehicle ruptured an effluent pipe. During repairs, about 15 tonnes of partially treated sewage entered Thornton Brook, which leads to the protected Mersey Estuary.
Environment Agency officers reported a sheen of oil on local waterways, while vegetation downstream of the refinery's discharge point was blackened by oil in January 2020.
The company was fined £80,000 for each of the 10 offences, with no additional penalty for the two 2019 incidents. Three breaches from 2022 and 2023 were taken into consideration without further punishment.
Nigel Glasgow, the Environment Agency's area environment manager, said the case showed "a repeated failure to comply" with permit conditions.
An EET Fuels spokesperson said: "We take our environmental responsibilities extremely seriously and regret these historic incidents."
The company said its investment included rerouting wastewater to United Utilities' Ellesmere Port treatment works, resulting in "a significant improvement in environmental performance", including fewer discharges and reduced freshwater use.

items.title: Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US
items.desc: Hundreds of young birds were also rescued from the fire, which comes as foie gras is under renewed scrutiny over animal welfare concerns.
items.text:
Flames engulfed Hudson Valley farm as 200 first responders arrived at the scene
A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.
The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.
Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.
Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.
Hudson Valley Farms is in a legal battle with the state of New York over its foie gras ban
Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.
"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.
The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.
Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.
The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.
Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.
New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.
At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.
Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.
Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.
The research, published in the journal Science Advances , involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.
The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.
The experiment is reminiscent of a plot point in the Christopher Nolan film Interstellar , in which a gravitational anomaly creates messages in binary code.
The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.
The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.
“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”
Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.
To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.

items.title: Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN
items.desc: Survivors reject relocation plans they say ignore their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
items.text:
Bududa has suffered repeated deadly landslides over the years
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; £3,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.
Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.
The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.

Johan Rockström, one of world’s leading climate experts, says slowing down scientific work puts cooperation at risk
Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.
Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems .
Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations.
Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].”
The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028. In the autumn of that year, nations will gather for Cop33, where the second “global stocktake” under the Paris agreement will be thrashed out.
This is the mechanism by which progress towards the core Paris goal, of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, will be judged. The stocktake is almost certain to find that current pledges to cut greenhouse gas emissions are inadequate and must be improved.
The UN has already found the world to be on track for a 2.8C temperature rise , a level previous IPCC reports have found would result in severe and, in some cases, irreversible consequences, such as the melting of ice caps and glaciers, sea level rises, coral bleaching and extreme weather.

The “sensational” discovery of a cave containing the skeletons of over 100 extinct cave bears has been revealed by local authorities.
Kept secret to prevent looting, the incredible assemblage of thousands of bones will remain tucked away behind iron bars until the spring thaw when an interdisciplinary team of scientists will begin studying them.
Discovered in July by a mountain guide in the Autonomous Province of South Tyrol, northern Italy, the cave sits around 9,100 feet above sea level on the side of an almost sheer cliff.
The guide, Kurt Walde, found the cave in the municipality of Enneberg just above another famous cave called Conturines, the highest in altitude in which cave bear remains had ever been found.
That cave was tragically looted before scientists had a chance to study all the animals that lived and died there. When Walde discovered this new, potentially even greater trove of extinct animal bones, Director of the Archeological Heritage Office, Christian Terzer, began work to construct a metal gate and protective tarp over the cave entrance to prevent similar illegal incursions.
“The logistical challenges of managing this project on a vertical rock face at almost 3000 meters above sea level were enormous,” Terzer said in a government statement.
The team was successful, however, and with winter closing in the site has been locked up until next June, when “an interdisciplinary research project with international participation, in which paleontologists, climate researchers, paleobotanists, speleologists, and specialists in ancient DNA will participate,” Terzer told Die Welt.
“With this safety operation, we are protecting not only an extraordinary site, but also the knowledge it contains. Now the scientific work begins, which will give us a more precise picture of how cave bears lived in the Dolomites,” added Provincial Councilor Philipp Achammer in the statement.
It’s unclear to scientists whether the cave hosted Ursus spelaeus or Ursus spelaeus ladinicus, two species of large bear known from Western Europe that lived during the Pleistocene, and which died out during the last Ice Age.
They were significantly larger than today’s brown bears, reaching more than 11 feet in length and standing 5.5 feet at the shoulder, yet they foraged almost exclusively on plant material. Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo: NASA/JPL-Caltech)
NASA’s Voyager 1 has made history. After nearly 50 years of travel, the spacecraft has reached one light-day from Earth. Launched Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 is humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, traveling through interstellar space at about 38,000 mph. Voyager 1 achieved the milestone on Nov. 18 at 5:16 a.m. EST.
Light-days, like light-years, measure distance, not time. To make sense of the vastness of space, scientists measure the amount of time it takes light to travel. According to NASA, light travels at about 186,000 miles per second in a vacuum. For comparison, sunlight passing Earth reaches the moon in 1.3 seconds. As such, a light-day measures the distance light travels in 24 hours, which is roughly 16.1 billion miles.
Mission engineers confirmed the light-day milestone using trajectory calculations and the probe’s carrier signal, which conveys data to Earth. Since Voyager’s radio signal travels at the speed of light, the astronomers in charge of the probe at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory heard from the probe 24 hours after achieving this feat.
Voyager 1, and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977, are the only probes built by humankind to ever go beyond our solar system. In 2012, Voyager became the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space after leaving the heliosphere , the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the sun that deflects cosmic radiation.
In addition to scientific instruments, Voyager 1 carries a Golden Record. Like a message in a bottle in an expansive ocean, the golden disc includes images and sounds from Earth, as well as inscriptions that show our planet’s location to any advanced civilization that may come across it.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” says Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”
